title: The Word of Life and the Light of God
summary: John opens by testifying that he and his companions heard, saw, and touched the Word of life, the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared in history. They proclaim it so that their readers may share fellowship with them and with the Father and the Son. Then comes the message: God is light, and walking with him means walking in the light, which includes honestly confessing sin and trusting God to forgive and cleanse.
story: The letter begins without a greeting, and it begins where John's Gospel begins, with the beginning. The Gospel told how the Word who was with God became flesh; this letter is written to people who already believe that, to strengthen them after some in their fellowship had left with a different account of who Jesus was. Chapter 1 lays the foundation for everything that follows: a real, physical Jesus witnessed by real people, and a holy God with whom sinners can nonetheless have fellowship. The claims John tests in verses 6, 8, and 10 anticipate the false teaching he will name more directly in chapter 2.
historical:
Christian tradition places the apostle John in Ephesus in his later years, and the letter is usually dated late in the first century, around AD 85 to 100. The churches John addressed had experienced a split. The people who left seem to have held a view of Jesus that downplayed or denied his full humanity, very likely an early form of what the church later called docetism, from the Greek dokeo, to seem: the belief that the divine Christ only appeared to be human. Irenaeus, writing about AD 180, reports that a teacher named Cerinthus, active in Asia in John's day, taught that the heavenly Christ came upon the man Jesus at his baptism and departed before his death.

Whatever its precise form, such teaching made the physical life of Jesus unimportant. John's opening, with its insistence on hearing, seeing, gazing upon, and touching, answers that directly. The eternal life of God was not a vision or an idea but a person who could be handled. The verbs are also a claim to eyewitness authority: the we of these verses are those who were there.
cultural:
Light and darkness were powerful images across the ancient world. In Greek philosophy, light often stood for knowledge and the divine mind; in some religious movements it stood for a spiritual realm set against the material one. The Dead Sea Scrolls, written by a Jewish sect before and during the time of Jesus, describe a struggle between the sons of light and the sons of darkness. John's statement that God is light draws on the Old Testament, where light is associated with God's presence, holiness, and truth (Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 60:19-20), and it has a moral edge: to walk in darkness is to live in sin and falsehood.

The word fellowship (koinonia) in the ancient world meant a partnership or shared possession, used of business partners, of marriage, and of friends who held things in common. John uses it for a shared life, first with the Father and the Son and then, as a result, with one another. Confession of sin had deep roots in Israel's worship, from the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:21) to the penitential psalms, and it was practiced in early Christian gatherings.
literary: The prologue (verses 1-4) is one long, crowded sentence in Greek, piling up relative clauses before it reaches its main verb, we proclaim. It echoes the prologue of John's Gospel: beginning, word, life, with the Father, revealed. The rest of the chapter is built on the message that God is light (verse 5), followed by three conditional sentences introduced by if we say (verses 6, 8, 10), each rejecting a false claim, and each followed by a true alternative (verses 7 and 9). The pattern of claim and counter-claim will run through the whole letter. John's style is simple in vocabulary and rich in repetition, circling a few great words: life, light, truth, fellowship, sin.

outline.t: The Word of life, heard, seen, and touched
God is light: walking in the light

doctrines.note: The Word of life was with the Father from the beginning and was revealed in history as a real, touchable human being. John grounds the faith in the incarnation, against any view that makes Jesus less than fully human.
God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. His holiness is complete and without mixture, and it sets the terms for fellowship with him.
John refuses both self-deception (claiming to have no sin) and despair. Sin is real in the believer's life, and denying it makes God out to be a liar.

The blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (verse 7), and God is faithful and just to forgive those who confess (verse 9). Forgiveness is just because it rests on Christ's sacrifice, not on overlooking sin.

words.note: Koinonia, fellowship, partnership, sharing. It appears four times in this chapter. It describes a common life held together, first with the Father and the Son and then with other believers. For John, fellowship is not a feeling of closeness but a real sharing in the life of God, with moral consequences.

Pselaphao, to touch or handle, sometimes used of groping in the dark. In verse 1 it stresses the physical reality of Jesus: the apostles did not merely see a vision but touched him with their hands. Luke 24:39 uses the same verb when the risen Jesus tells his disciples to touch him and see that he has flesh and bones.

Homologeo, to confess, literally to say the same thing. To confess sins is to agree with God about them, calling them what he calls them. The same verb is used later in the letter for confessing Jesus as the Son of God come in the flesh.

christ: The chapter's opening is one of the New Testament's strongest witnesses to the incarnation. The eternal life that was with the Father became visible and touchable in Jesus, whom the apostles knew in the ordinary ways of hearing and handling. John calls him the Word of life, echoing John 1:1 and 1:14, and identifies him as the Son of the Father. The chapter also shows what Christ has done: his blood cleanses from all sin. The one who shared real flesh shed real blood, and it is that death, not a spiritual idea, that makes fellowship with the holy God possible for sinners.

hard.q: If believers are already forgiven through Christ, why do they need to keep confessing their sins?
hard.a:
The question is fair, since the New Testament teaches that those in Christ are justified once and for all (Romans 5:1; 8:1). Christians have generally answered by distinguishing between the standing of a believer before God and the ongoing relationship. Justification, God's declaration that a sinner is righteous through Christ, does not need to be repeated. But fellowship, the daily walk with God, is affected by sin, and confession restores it, much as a child who has wronged a parent remains a child but needs to set things right. Jesus taught his disciples to ask the Father to forgive their debts as a regular part of prayer.

Others add that verse 9 is not describing a new transaction each time but the ongoing character of the Christian life: those who walk in the light keep agreeing with God about their sin, and they keep finding that his forgiveness holds. Either way, John's point is pastoral. The alternative to confession is not a higher spirituality but self-deception.

questions: John stresses that the apostles heard, saw, and touched Jesus. Why does it matter that the Christian faith rests on a real person in history rather than an idea or experience?
Which of the three false claims in verses 6, 8, and 10 are you most tempted to make, and what would honest confession look like for you?
How does knowing that God is faithful and just to forgive change the way you approach him after you fail?
